observed_title: Empirical Process Sampled Along a Stationary Process

read_ranges.scope: Full article read: title/abstract, Sections 1–4, every displayed proof and example, and references (42 PDF pages). Key formulas and theorem statements visually checked on pp.7–15, 17–21, 24–27, 29–36, 38 and 40.

topic_relevance.K04: adjacent. The paper studies empirical CDF/processes sampled along deterministic sequences and ergodic cocycles, proving qualitative Glivenko–Cantelli and weak FCLT results under local-time/self-intersection conditions. It supplies a useful condition-checking and limit-process component, but has no anti-concentration inequality for a supremum and no quantitative Gaussian coupling error. Weak convergence alone does not imply a high-threshold tail approximation or a small-interval probability bound.

definitions.name: Sampled empirical process and occupation counts
definitions.statement: For a sequence z_0,…,z_{n−1} in Z^d, N_n(ℓ)=#{0≤k<n:z_k=ℓ}, M_n=max_ℓ N_n(ℓ), and V_n=Σ_ℓN_n(ℓ)^2=#{(j,k):z_j=z_k}. For a random field X_ℓ with common cdf F, W_n(s)=Σ_{k<n}(1{X_{z_k}≤s}−F(s)). Thus V_n measures self-intersections and M_n the largest multiplicity.

source_ranges.scope: PDF pp.2–3: empirical-process setup, N_n, M_n, V_n and identities.

definitions.name: Cocycle and cylinder map
definitions.statement: For ergodic (X,B,µ,T) and f:X→Z^d, f_k(x)=Σ_{j<k}f(T^jx). The occupation N_n(x,ℓ), M_n(x), V_n(x) are defined from the first n cocycle positions. The cylinder map is T̃_f(x,ℓ)=(Tx,ℓ+f(x)); its orbit sums of 1_{X×{0}} recover N_n(x,ℓ).

source_ranges.scope: PDF p.16: definitions and occupation-count interpretation.

definitions.name: Empirical-process variance kernel
definitions.statement: K_n(t)=|Σ_{k<n}e^{2πi⟨z_k,t⟩}|²=|Σ_ℓN_n(ℓ)e^{2πi⟨ℓ,t⟩}|². For stationary centered fields with absolutely summable correlations and spectral density ρ, E|Σ_{k<n}X_{z_k}|²=∫_{T^d}K_n(t)ρ(t)dt≤||ρ||_∞V_n.

source_ranges.scope: PDF p.13, equation (17) and covariance-kernel bound.

theorem_cards.label: Propositions 1.2 and 1.4 (pointwise bounds for sampled sums)
assumptions: For Proposition 1.2, the field U_ℓ is centered and uniformly bounded; V_n≤C_1 n²/(log n)^β.
For Proposition 1.2, either the uniform absolute covariance sum is finite and β>1, or the field is stationary, Σ_ℓ|⟨U_ℓ,U_0⟩|^ζ<∞ for ζ∈[1,2], and β>ζ.

For Proposition 1.4(1), U_ℓ are iid, centered, uniformly bounded by K, with E|U_0|²=1; for (2), they are stationary centered associated variables; the sharper second part assumes summable correlations.
theorem_cards.statement: Proposition 1.2 gives S_n/n→0 almost surely under either covariance/local-time regime. Proposition 1.4(1) gives limsup_n |S_n|/[√(V_n·2loglog n)]≤K a.s., hence S_n/n→0 if V_n=o(n²/loglog n). In the associated case, with σ_n²=E|S_n|², limsup |S_n|/[σ_n(logσ_n)^(1/2+ε)]≤1; if correlations are summable then |S_n|=O(√V_n(log n)^(1/2+ε)) a.s.
proof_steps: For Proposition 1.2, bound the second moment by V_n times the covariance sum, use a geometric subsequence and Borel–Cantelli, then fill gaps using bounded increments. In the stationary ζ<2 branch, split the spectral density at a cutoff M_n and balance the two terms.
For iid variables, apply Hoeffding to the independent weighted variables N_n(ℓ)U_ℓ; for associated variables, use Newman–Wright’s maximal inequality and a subsequence in σ_n.

proof_source_ranges.scope: Proof of Proposition 1.2, including the spectral split and subsequence step.
Proof of Proposition 1.4: associated maximal inequality and iid Hoeffding/Borel–Cantelli branches.

gaps: The Newman–Wright maximal inequality and Hoeffding inputs are cited, not proved here. The constant K in the iid LIL-type bound is the uniform envelope and is not dimension/entropy information for a supremum over functions.

theorem_cards.label: Theorems 1.5–1.8 (Glivenko–Cantelli along a sampled sequence)
assumptions: Let V_n≤C_1 n²/(log n)^β. The stationary field mixing coefficient is γ(ℓ) as defined in (14).
For Theorem 1.6(a), the field is iid and V_n=o(n²/loglog n). For (b), it is strictly stationary and associated, has summable covariances, and V_n=O(n²(log n)^(−1−η)) for some η>0.
For Proposition 1.7/Theorem 1.8, the field is centered, strictly stationary, and pairwise-PQD with summable covariance; sampling has maximal local time M_n and satisfies Σ_n M_n/n²<∞.
theorem_cards.statement: Theorem 1.5 yields a sampled Glivenko–Cantelli theorem if Σ_ℓγ(ℓ)<∞ and β>1, or if the field is stationary, Σ_ℓγ(ℓ)^ζ<∞ for ζ∈[1,2], and β>ζ. Theorem 1.6 gives the iid and associated sufficient conditions above. Under the stated PQD conditions, Proposition 1.7 gives a.s. convergence of centered sums/n; Theorem 1.8 gives pointwise empirical-cdf convergence at continuity points, uniform in s if F is continuous.
proof_steps: The mixing branch bounds indicator covariances by γ(ℓ) and invokes Proposition 1.2. The iid branch uses Proposition 1.4 and a countable dense set of continuity points plus jump control. For associated fields, smoothed step functions and Hoeffding’s covariance identity transfer the pointwise bound to indicators. The PQD branch uses a cited strong law and the local-time summability condition.
The dense-set argument is converted to uniform convergence using Lemma 1.1; continuity of F is required for the stated uniform-in-s conclusion in the associated/PQD cases.

proof_source_ranges.scope: Theorem 1.5–1.6 statements and proof of Theorem 1.6(a,b), PDF pp.10–11.
Proposition 1.7, Theorem 1.8, and associated/PQD smoothing arguments, PDF p.12.

gaps: The proof imports Lemma 1.1, Hoeffding’s covariance identity, and a PQD strong law from cited sources. These are not quantitative rates for the empirical cdf.

theorem_cards.label: Theorem 1.9 (iid sampled empirical-process FCLT)
assumptions: The field (X_ℓ)_{ℓ∈Z^d} is iid with common cdf F supported on [0,1]; z_k is a deterministic sequence with occupation counts N_n and self-intersection count V_n.
The maximal multiplicity condition is M_n²/V_n→0.
theorem_cards.statement: With Y_n(s)=V_n^(−1/2)Σ_{k<n}(1{X_{z_k}≤s}−F(s))=V_n^(−1/2)Σ_ℓN_n(ℓ)(1{X_ℓ≤s}−F(s)), one has Y_n⇒W^0∘F in D[0,1], where W^0 is a standard Brownian bridge.
proof_steps: Use Cramér–Wold and Lindeberg for finite-dimensional convergence; the maximal-weight condition is max_ℓN_n(ℓ)/√V_n→0. Covariances match F(s∧t)−F(s)F(t).

For continuous F, prove tightness via a uniform fourth-moment bound on two adjacent increments, expanding into same-site and distinct-site terms and bounding each by the squared F-mass of the combined interval.
For general F, pass through a generalized inverse from the uniform empirical process; no quantitative rate is obtained.

proof_source_ranges.scope: Finite-dimensional Lindeberg proof and covariance calculation, PDF p.14.
Tightness and generalized-inverse argument, PDF p.15.

gaps: The conclusion is weak convergence only; it supplies neither a Gaussian approximation error nor an anti-concentration bound for sup_s Y_n(s). Tightness cites Billingsley.

theorem_cards.label: Lemmas 2.2–2.3 (range, multiplicity and self-intersection identities)
assumptions: z_k is any sequence in Z^d; in the cocycle specialization, f_k(x)=Σ_{j<k}f(T^jx).
theorem_cards.statement: For nonempty A⊂Z^d, V_n≥(Σ_{k<n}1_{z_k∈A})²/|A|, hence for a cocycle V_n(x)≥n²/|R_n(x)|. The cocycle identities give V_n=n+2Σ_{k=1}^{n−1}Σ_{j=0}^{n−k−1}1_{f_k(T^jx)=0} and M_n(x)≤1+max_{0≤k<n}N_n(T^kx,0), plus one-step recursions for V_n and M_n.
proof_steps: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the number of visits in A and the counts at each site.
Use the cocycle identity f_k(x)=f(x)+f_{k−1}(Tx) to derive the occupation recursion; sum squared counts for V_n and start at a maximally visited site for the bound on M_n.

proof_source_ranges.scope: Statements and full proofs of Lemmas 2.2–2.3, PDF pp.17–18.

gaps: These are deterministic/cocycle occupancy facts; no empirical-process tail estimate follows without additional assumptions.

theorem_cards.label: Propositions 2.6–2.7 (coboundary dichotomy for V_n/n²)
assumptions: T is ergodic and f:X→Z^d is an integrable cocycle.
theorem_cards.statement: If f is a coboundary, then lim_n V_n(x)/n²=β>0 a.e. and liminf M_n(x)/n>0. In general a constant β≥0 exists with V_n(x)/n²→β a.e.; β>0 if and only if (T,f) is a coboundary. Thus a non-coboundary cocycle has V_n/n²→0 a.e.
proof_steps: In the coboundary case f=TΦ−Φ, reduce occupation counts to Birkhoff averages of level sets Φ=ℓ and exhaust Z^d by finite balls.

In the non-coboundary case, express V_n/n² through return counts to zero for the cylinder map; use the infinite-measure ergodic theorem, tail maximal functions and the classical maximal inequality to show the normalized collision term vanishes. Lemma 2.5 and ergodicity yield an a.s. constant limit.
gaps: The identification that the invariant cylinder-map density is zero for a non-coboundary cocycle cites Conze [12], not reproved in this paper.

theorem_cards.label: Proposition 3.2 (positive asymptotic variance profile for transient walks)
assumptions: Z is a transient, aperiodic, non-deterministic random walk on Z^d. For the variance conclusion, ρ is a nonzero continuous nonnegative spectral density of a stationary centered random field with absolutely summable correlations.
theorem_cards.statement: With Ψ(t)=E exp(2πi⟨ζ_0,t⟩) and Φ(t)=(1−|Ψ(t)|²)/|1−Ψ(t)|² away from 0 (Φ(0)=0), there is M≥0 such that the Fourier coefficients of n^(−1)K_n converge to those of Φ+Mδ_0. Consequently, the normalized variance ∫_{T^d}n^(−1)K_n(t)ρ(t)dt has a strictly positive limit.
proof_steps: For each lattice point ℓ, transience gives a finite Green-function sum I(ℓ)=1_{ℓ=0}+Σ_{k≥1}[P(Z_k=ℓ)+P(Z_k=−ℓ)]. The ergodic averaging lemma identifies these as limits of the Fourier coefficients of n^(−1)K_n.

Introduce the Abel-regularized profile Φ_λ=(1−λ²|Ψ|²)/|1−λΨ|². Let λ↑1; Fatou at ℓ=0 gives Φ∈L¹ and a possible nonnegative residual mass M at the origin. Aperiodicity bounds Φ_λ off a neighborhood of 0; near 0, positivity and cos(2π⟨ℓ,t⟩)≈1 identify the same residual mass for each Fourier coefficient.

The nonnegative kernels have bounded L¹ norm, so coefficient convergence yields convergence against continuous ρ and the limit ∫Φρ+Mρ(0)>0. The paper notes that M=0 for d>1 as an external result from Spitzer, not as part of this proof.

proof_source_ranges.scope: Proof setup: Green-function coefficients and Abel-regularized identity, PDF p.29–30.
Control near t=0 and positive limiting variance profile, PDF p.31.

gaps: The statement is a variance/covariance result for transient random-walk sampling, not a supremum anti-concentration result. The claim M=0 for d>1 is cited from [28] and not proved in this article.

theorem_cards.label: Lemma 3.3 and Lemma 3.4 (local-time bounds from LLT / finite-coordinate dependence)
assumptions: Lemma 3.3 assumes a local limit theorem for a two-dimensional cocycle.
Lemma 3.4 assumes a Bernoulli scheme over a finite alphabet and a centered Z^d-valued function depending on finitely many coordinates.
theorem_cards.statement: Under the d=2 LLT, for every ε>0 there is integrable C(x) with N_n(x,0)≤C(x)(log n)^(2+ε) and V_n(x)≤C(x)n(log n)^(2+ε). In the finite-coordinate Bernoulli setting, the integrated mth local-time moments satisfy ∫N_n(·,ℓ)^m dµ≤C_m n^(m/2) for d=1 and ≤C′_m(log n)^m for d=2, with constants independent of ℓ.
proof_steps: For Lemma 3.3, sum the LLT return-probability bounds to obtain an integrable weighted square series, then use dyadic interpolation for N_n and the occupation identity for V_n.

For Lemma 3.4, expand the mth moment over ordered visit times; finite coordinate dependence leaves separated blocks independent. Bound the resulting convolution by powers of the maximal point probability and invoke the random-walk LLT estimates.
gaps: The LLT premise and the convolution/point-probability estimates are imported from cited random-walk or dynamical-system literature; the article does not establish a general LLT.

theorem_cards.label: Lemma 3.5 and Example 3.6 (a rotation sequence satisfying the FCLT criterion)
assumptions: For Lemma 3.5, z_1,…,z_n are real-valued and σ_n²=n^(−1)Σ_k(z_k−m_n)² with m_n=n^(−1)Σ_k z_k.
Example 3.6 assumes an irrational rotation α with bounded partial quotients and f=1_[0,1/2)−1_[1/2,1), with the cited occupation estimate (50).
theorem_cards.statement: If σ_n>1, V_n≥9n²/(80σ_n). For the stated bounded-variation rotation cocycle, an external cited estimate gives sup_x N_n(x,0)≲n/√log n; the paper then derives M_n(x)≲n/√log n and V_n(x)≲n²/√log n, while the variance-based lower bound gives matching orders up to constants. Consequently M_n²/V_n≲1/√log n→0, so Theorem 1.9 applies; Theorem 1.6(a) also gives sampled Glivenko–Cantelli for iid field values.
proof_steps: For Lemma 3.5, Chebyshev’s inequality shows at least a fixed fraction of z_k lies in an interval of length O(σ_n); apply the range/occupation Cauchy–Schwarz bound.
In Example 3.6, combine the rotation local-time estimate with M_n≤1+max_kN_n(T^kx,0), V_n≤nM_n, and the variance lower bound to verify the strict ratio condition.

proof_source_ranges.scope: The rotation estimates and Example 3.6 conclusion, PDF p.36.

gaps: The key upper bound (50) is attributed to Aaronson–Bromberg–Nakada [1]; this paper only explains how to upgrade essential-supremum to uniform supremum. The criterion is for this special rotation/cocycle, not arbitrary sampling paths.

theorem_cards.label: Proposition 4.1 and Lemma 4.2 (ergodic skew-product route to sampled GC)
assumptions: T is an ergodic probability-preserving map, f:X→Z^d a cocycle, and θ a measure-preserving Z^d-action on (Ω,P); ϕ∈L¹(µ×P).

For the ordinary-distribution centering, additionally require the skew product T_{θ,f} to be ergodic. The sufficient criterion in Lemma 4.2 assumes the cocycle is recurrent, the cylinder map is ergodic, and the θ-action is ergodic.
theorem_cards.statement: The ergodic theorem for T_{θ,f}(x,ω)=(Tx,θ_{f(x)}ω), followed by the cited Tucker uniformization and Fubini, gives for µ-a.e. x a P-a.s. Glivenko–Cantelli convergence to the conditional expectation over T_{θ,f}-invariant sets. If T_{θ,f} is ergodic, the centering reduces to F(s)=µ×P{ϕ≤s}. Under Lemma 4.2’s conditions, T_{θ,f} is ergodic.
proof_steps: Apply the pointwise ergodic theorem for each half-line indicator; invoke Tucker’s result to make convergence uniform in s, then use Fubini to obtain the sampled statement for almost every x.
For Lemma 4.2, lift a T_{θ,f}-invariant function to X×Z^d along the θ-action; cylinder-map ergodicity makes it constant in (x,ℓ), and θ-ergodicity forces the remaining function to be constant.

proof_source_ranges.scope: Skew-product ergodic theorem, Proposition 4.1 and statement, PDF p.38.

gaps: Uniformization is cited to Tucker [29]. The route is qualitative and requires ergodicity of the specific skew product for ordinary centering; it is not a coupling or anti-concentration argument.

theorem_cards.label: Proposition 4.3 (bounded-growth universal averaging for Lebesgue spectrum)
assumptions: z_k is a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers satisfying z_k≤Ck, and the dynamical system has Lebesgue spectrum.
theorem_cards.statement: Then z_k is pointwise good for the class of Lebesgue-spectrum systems: for every ϕ∈L¹(P), n^(−1)Σ_{k<n}ϕ∘θ_{z_k} converges almost surely.
proof_steps: Use the SLLN for orthogonal variables on a dense subspace of L², then density in L¹ and closure of the convergence class under the ergodic maximal lemma using z_k≤Ck.

proof_source_ranges.scope: Statement and proof of Proposition 4.3, PDF p.40.

gaps: This is a class-specific universal averaging statement, not a result about anti-concentration or a Gaussian empirical-process supremum.

constant_dependence: Proposition 1.2 constants depend on the uniform covariance-sum/spectral-density bounds and sequence constant C_1; the cutoff and logarithmic exponent depend on ζ,β.
Proposition 1.4 constants depend on the uniform bound K, variance normalization, covariance sum, and ε; these are pointwise sum bounds, not entropy constants.
Theorem 1.9 states convergence under M_n²/V_n→0 and supplies no rate or coupling constant.
Theorem 1.5–1.8 conditions retain their displayed C_1, β, ζ, η and covariance/mixing sums; they do not give an anti-concentration constant.
Lemma 3.3 constants depend on ε and are integrable random variables; Lemma 3.4 constants depend on m and finite-coordinate support; rotation constants depend on α and f.
endpoint_limits: Theorem 1.9 is iid in the spatial field and uses the strict asymptotic condition M_n²/V_n→0; no rate is asserted. General F is handled by a generalized inverse, and the limit is W⁰∘F.
Uniform-in-s GC is stated when F is continuous; for discontinuous cdf, the theorem provides convergence at continuity points and explicitly handles the countable jump set.
Association and pairwise-PQD are distinct dependence assumptions: the PQD route has the stronger local-time summability Σ M_n/n²<∞.
For cocycles, V_n/n² has positive limit exactly in the coboundary case. A non-coboundary cocycle only forces that ratio to zero, not the stronger M_n²/V_n→0 FCLT condition.
Rotation example 3.6 is a special bounded-partial-quotient, bounded-variation construction; its local-time upper bound does not apply to general centered cocycles or arbitrary stationary fields.
The paper explicitly constructs transient and recurrent cocycle counterexamples to show M_n²/V_n→0 need not hold automatically.
reusable_methods: Reduce a sampled empirical process to weighted iid summands with weights N_n(ℓ); the exact variance is V_n times the Brownian-bridge covariance, and max-weight/√V_n controls Lindeberg.
Use the occupation triple (N_n,M_n,V_n) to separate maximal multiplicity from total self-intersection; apply V_n≥n²/|range| and M_n≤1+max shifted return count.
For dependence classes, smooth half-line indicators, use covariance identities to transfer pointwise sum bounds, and then pass from a countable dense set plus jumps to uniform cdf convergence.

Use the Fourier kernel K_n and spectral density to calculate variances for stationary fields; in transient random walks, the Abel-regularized characteristic-function kernel identifies a limiting nonnegative spectral profile.
Use induced maps and roof functions over rotations to construct examples where local-time ratios fail or hold, illustrating that transience/recurrence alone does not settle the FCLT criterion.
Use skew products to turn a pointwise ergodic theorem into a sampled Glivenko–Cantelli statement, while retaining conditional centering unless the skew product is ergodic.
unchecked: External inputs were not independently read/proved here: Newman–Wright maximal inequality [27], Hoeffding covariance identity [2], Birkel PQD strong law [4], Chung uniformization Lemma 1.1 [7], Billingsley tightness/inverse arguments [3], Tucker uniform GC theorem [29], and general range/cylinder-map results [14],[12].
The local-limit bounds for Bernoulli/Markov cocycles and the occupation estimates cited in Section 3 ([18],[19],[11]) are not independently verified.
The bounded-variation rotation estimate (50) is imported from Aaronson–Bromberg–Nakada [1]; only the stated upgrade from essential to uniform supremum is shown here.
Random-walk maximum/local-time asymptotics cited from Erdős–Taylor, Kesten, and Dembo–Peres–Rosen–Zeitouni [15],[16],[22] are survey inputs and are not proved in this article.
The source is fully read, but reading is not an independent proof audit; no result here yields the K04 anti-concentration or quantitative Gaussian-coupling step.
